===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a polished, fully offline iOS trip-planning app called "Waypoint".
Native Apple stack only: SwiftUI + SwiftData for persistence, MapKit for
all mapping, ActivityKit for Live Activities, EventKit for calendar
export. No backend, no accounts, no third-party SDKs, no network calls
except on-device MapKit/local geocoding (which works offline-cached but
may need network for tile fetch — if a feature would require live
network for correctness, don't fake it; record it as a gap). Follow the
ios-app-factory-rules.

Core features (complete over broad — ship fewer things fully working):

1. Trips & itinerary: create trips with a date range; each trip has
   multiple days; each day has an ordered list of stops (place name,
   address, optional MapKit-resolved coordinate, time window, notes,
   category icon). Reorder stops via drag-and-drop within a day AND
   across days. Get date math right across the trip's date range,
   including a trip that starts and ends on the same day and a
   single-day trip.

2. Map view: a MapKit view per day showing all of that day's stops as
   annotations connected by a route line (MKDirections walking/driving,
   gracefully degrading to a straight-line polyline with a visible
   "approximate" indicator if MKDirections has no network). Tapping a
   stop centers the map and highlights it; tapping a map pin selects
   the corresponding itinerary row (two-way binding).

3. Expense splitting: a per-trip list of travelers (name, no accounts).
   Log expenses (amount, payer, split method: equal / exact amounts /
   percentage) against any subset of travelers. A settle-up screen
   computing the minimum set of payments to zero every balance (the
   classic debt-simplification graph problem — get this genuinely
   correct, including rounding remainders so amounts always sum
   exactly). Use Decimal, never Double, for money.

4. Packing lists: per-trip checklist, templates the user can save and
   reapply to future trips, a "packed %" indicator.

5. Live Activity: while a trip is "active" (today falls within its date
   range), a Live Activity / Dynamic Island showing the current or next
   stop and time until it, updating as stops are checked off. Must
   degrade gracefully (no crash, no Live Activity) on devices/OS
   versions without support, and when the user denies the permission.

6. Calendar export: export a day's stops as EventKit calendar events
   (with the user's explicit permission), one event per stop honoring
   its time window; must not create duplicate events if exported twice
   for the same day — detect and either skip or update existing ones.

7. Home-screen widget (WidgetKit, separate target): shows the active
   trip's next stop, or "no active trip" honestly if none.

8. iPad: itinerary list and map must work as a genuine two-column split
   view on iPad, not just a stretched phone layout.

Priorities: the debt-simplification math, the drag-reorder data
integrity (no duplicate/lost stops across days), and honest degradation
of every system-permission-gated feature (Live Activities, Calendar,
location) — never fake success when a permission is denied or a
capability is unavailable in the Simulator. Explicitly call out in a
Gaps section anything requiring infrastructure this project can't
provide (live traffic data, real-time flight tracking, iCloud trip
sync). Seed a "demo trip" toggle in Settings with realistic multi-day
sample data so no screen is empty on first review. Provide a clear way
to run it in the iOS Simulator via Xcode.

===== PHASE PLAYBOOK (editable phase_rules.json) =====
Global app-build rules:
- Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.
- The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.
- Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
- Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.
- Empty states are designed content (icon + one-line explanation + the action that fills the screen), never a blank view or bare 'No data' text.
- No default unstyled List, Form, or navigation chrome where the design spec calls for custom rows, cards, or backgrounds; the built UI must match the spec.
- Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
- Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

Phase rules:
- Preserve the user's original prompt before interpreting it.
- Convert the prompt into hard requirements, non-goals, output shape, quality bar, and decision rules.
- Resolve conflicts by naming the assumption, not by silently changing the assignment.

Required output:
- Original prompt excerpt or full prompt reference.
- Hard requirements.
- Non-goals.
- Production-readiness definition.
- Decision rules for later phases.
- A NUMBERED list of testable requirements extracted from the user's prompt — each one verifiable by using the app.

Acceptance checks before consensus:
- A later phase can tell whether it is violating the user's prompt.
- Multi-app quantity/category requirements are explicit.
- Production-ready means more than a prototype or spec.
- Every promise in the original prompt maps to a numbered requirement; nothing is silently dropped.


===== RELEVANT KNOWLEDGE (curated IOS reference — use it, don't restate it) =====

----- Apple Frameworks Cheatsheet -----
# First-Party Apple Frameworks Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / Swift 5.9+)

Build capable iPhone apps with **zero third-party dependencies**. For each framework: when to reach for it, the entry-point type, and a compilable, idiomatic snippet or the gotcha that bites people. All examples target **iOS 17 minimum** unless a call-out says otherwise; Swift Concurrency (`async`/`await`) is preferred over completion handlers everywhere Apple offers it.

## General rules

- **Prefer these over SPM packages.** RevenueCat, Firebase Analytics, Lottie, Alamofire, etc. all have first-party equivalents good enough for most apps. Fewer deps = smaller binary, faster builds, no supply-chain risk, no privacy-manifest surprises.
- **Every framework that touches user data needs an `Info.plist` usage-description string** (or an entitlement). Missing it is a runtime crash the moment the API is used — not a compile error. The specific keys are listed per section.
- **Import the framework and its SwiftUI companion when one exists** (e.g. `import MapKit` gives you `Map`; `import StoreKit` gives you `SubscriptionStoreView`/`StoreView`).
- **Do capability checks before hardware-dependent APIs** (`CHHapticEngine.capabilitiesForHardware().supportsHaptics`, `HKHealthStore.isHealthDataAvailable()`, `GKLocalPlayer.local.isAuthenticated`). Simulators and older/cheaper devices lie.
- **Never block the main actor.** Long queries, audio-graph setup, and StoreKit calls belong in `Task {}` or `async` functions.
- **Verify APIs against the deployment target.** Several SwiftUI conveniences (e.g. `GameCenterView`, Control widgets) shipped *after* iOS 17. Availability call-outs below flag these.

---

## StoreKit 2 — In-App Purchase & Subscriptions

**Use it when:** you sell anything — consumables, non-consumables, or auto-renewable subscriptions. Replaces callback-based StoreKit 1 entirely.

**Start from:** `Product` (fetch + purchase) and `Transaction` (entitlements + history). No server strictly required — signatures are verified on-device via `VerificationResult`.

### The three things you must do

1. **Load products by ID** (IDs come from App Store Connect):

```swift
import StoreKit

let productIDs = ["com.app.pro.monthly", "com.app.pro.yearly", "com.app.coins.100"]
let products = try await Product.products(for: productIDs)   // async throws
```

2. **Purchase, then verify and finish the transaction:**

```swift
func purchase(_ product: Product) async throws -> Transaction? {
    let result = try await product.purchase()
    switch result {
    case .success(let verification):
        let transaction = try checkVerified(verification)
        await transaction.finish()          // REQUIRED — unfinished txns replay forever
        return transaction
    case .userCancelled, .pending:
        return nil
    @unknown default:
        return nil
    }
}

func checkVerified<T>(_ result: VerificationResult<T>) throws -> T {
    switch result {
    case .unverified(_, let error): throw error   // signature failed — do NOT grant
    case .verified(let safe):       return safe
    }
}
```

3. **Listen for `Transaction.updates` from app launch** — the single most-missed requirement. It catches renewals, Ask-to-Buy approvals, refunds, and purchases made on other devices.

```swift
// Start this in your App init / a top-level task and keep it alive for the app's lifetime.
func observeTransactions() -> Task<Void, Never> {
    Task.detached {
        for await update in Transaction.updates {
            guard case .verified(let transaction) = update else { continue }
            await grantEntitlement(for: transaction)   // your unlock logic
            await transaction.finish()
        }
    }
}
```

### Checking what the user currently owns

Use `Transaction.currentEntitlements` (an async sequence). **iOS 18.4+ note:** the per-product `Transaction.currentEntitlement(for:)` is deprecated in favor of `Transaction.currentEntitlements(for:)`, because a user can hold multiple entitling transactions (e.g. own it *and* have Family Sharing access).

```swift
func hasActiveSubscription() async -> Bool {
    for await result in Transaction.currentEntitlements {
        guard case .verified(let transaction) = result else { continue }
        if transaction.productType == .autoRenewable && transaction.revocationDate == nil {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}
```

### Subscription status & renewal info

```swift
// groupID = the subscription group configured in App Store Connect
let statuses = try await Product.SubscriptionInfo.status(for: subscriptionGroupID)
for status in statuses {
    guard case .verified(let renewalInfo) = status.renewalInfo else { continue }
    let willAutoRenew = renewalInfo.willAutoRenew   // false => user cancelled, still in period
    _ = (status.state, willAutoRenew)               // .subscribed, .expired, .inGracePeriod, ...
}
```

### Drop-in SwiftUI storefront (iOS 17+)

Skip building a custom paywall — these render Apple's native UI:

```swift
import SwiftUI
import StoreKit

// Whole subscription group with a marketing header:
SubscriptionStoreView(groupID: subscriptionGroupID) {
    VStack { Text("Unlock Pro").font(.largeTitle.bold()) }
}
.subscriptionStoreControlStyle(.prominentPicker)

// Non-subscription products:
StoreView(ids: ["com.app.coins.100", "com.app.coins.500"])
```

### Gotchas

- **Test locally with a `.storekit` configuration file** (Xcode → File → New → File → StoreKit Configuration). Lets you buy, refund, and fast-forward renewals in the simulator with no sandbox account.
- `await transaction.finish()` is mandatory — forgetting it makes the transaction reappear in `Transaction.updates` every launch.
- **Always ship a "Restore Purchases" button** for non-consumables/subscriptions (App Review requirement). Call `try await AppStore.sync()`, then re-scan `currentEntitlements`.
- **Consumables are not in `currentEntitlements`** — grant them at p

Seed a "demo trip" toggle in Settings with realistic multi-day sample data so no screen is empty on first review. Provide a clear way to run it in the iOS Simulator via Xcode."

Now my read on this, wearing the QA/skeptic hat.

The biggest thing I want locked down before anyone starts building is that this prompt already names its own hardest failure modes, and later phases will be tempted to declare success on the easy 80% and hand-wave the rest. My job is to make sure "done" can't be claimed without evidence on exactly the parts that are easy to fake. Three areas deserve genuinely adversarial test cases, not just implementation:

Debt simplification is the one I trust least by default. "Minimum set of payments" is a real graph-reduction problem (greedy max-debtor/max-creditor settlement), and it's very easy to ship something that merely computes correct net balances but pays everyone individually instead of minimizing transactions — that would look right in a two-person test and be wrong the moment there are four or five travelers. The rounding requirement is the sharper trap: splitting $100 three ways in Decimal gives 33.33/33.33/33.34, and whoever eats the extra cent needs a deterministic, stated rule, not whichever traveler happens to be last in an array. I want a decision rule now: remainder cents go to a specific, documented position (e.g., first payer alphabetically, or the person who paid), and the sum of all splits for any expense must equal the original amount exactly, checked in code, not by eyeballing. Also: what happens when percentages entered by the user don't sum to 100, or an expense is split across a subset of travelers where the payer isn't included in the split? Those are testable edge cases and none of them can be quietly skipped.

Drag-and-drop reorder across days is the second trust-nothing area. "No duplicate/lost stops" sounds like a UI nicety but it's actually a data-model correctness question — moving a stop from Day 2 to Day 4 has to be one atomic operation on the SwiftData graph, not a delete-then-insert that can leave orphans if the app is backgrounded mid-drag. I'd also flag: when a stop moves to a different day, does its time window travel with it (probably now nonsensical if the trip's days have different structure) or get cleared? The prompt doesn't say, so I want that named as an assumption in the contract rather than decided silently later — my default vote is the time window is preserved as entered but the UI must visually flag it if it now falls outside typical hours, since silently clearing user data is its own bug.

The third area is honest degradation, and this is where I'm most skeptical of what a build phase will claim. Live Activities cannot be fully verified in the Simulator the way they render on-device with the actual Dynamic Island, and "today falls within the trip's date range" needs a single injected notion of "now" so it's actually testable without waiting for real calendar days to pass — I want a debug/demo-data hook for that, but it must never leak into what looks like real user data (that directly collides with the global rule against showing sample data as if it's real, so the demo trip needs a visible, unmistakable "Demo" marker, not just realistic content). Permission-denial paths for Live Activities, Calendar, and any location/geocoding prompt need to be exercised by actually denying the permission in the Simulator and confirming the app doesn't crash and doesn't silently claim success — a checkbox that says "exported to Calendar" when EventKit access was never granted is exactly the kind of lie this app must never tell. Calendar export dedup also needs a concrete mechanism, not a promise: store the EventKit event identifier per stop at export time, and on re-export, look it up and update in place; and handle the case where the user deleted the event externally, or revoked Calendar access between exports.

I'd also push back preemptively on one thing that's easy to sneak in by default: SwiftData very commonly gets scaffolded with CloudKit sync turned on. This app is explicitly "no accounts, no backend," and iCloud trip sync is named as an out-of-scope gap, so CloudKit sync must be off by default, not left enabled and undocumented. Similarly, ActivityKit's live-update path most naturally uses push tokens from a server — since there's no backend, Live Activity updates must be local/scheduled only, and that constraint should be stated explicitly so nobody quietly reaches for a push-based update mechanism that would require the backend the prompt forbids.

For the widget: WidgetKit timelines are refreshed on a budget, not in real time, so "shows the active trip's next stop" needs an honest framing — it will be accurate as of its last refresh, and that's a real constraint worth stating up front rather than discovering when the widget looks stale during review.

On iPad, "genuine two-column split view" should be verified at more than one iPad size and in both orientations, plus a check that it isn't just a `NavigationSplitView` wrapper that collapses to the same single-column phone layout under Slide Over — that's a common way to technically satisfy the letter of the requirement while missing the spirit.

Production-readiness, in my view, means every one of the above degradation paths has actually been exercised and observed to fail gracefully — not "the code has a guard clause," but "someone denied the permission / disabled network / ran on iPad in portrait and slide-over and watched what happened." A build-verification phase that only compiles and runs the happy path hasn't earned the right to call this done.

Decision rule I want carried forward: whenever a later phase hits a case the prompt didn't specify (remainder-cent assignment, what happens to a stop's time window on cross-day move, what "no active trip" widget state looks like visually), it must write down the assumption it made rather than pick silently — because these are exactly the seams where "looks done" and "is actually correct" diverge, and the whole point of naming me QA/skeptic this round is to make sure nobody gets to average those two together.
